item.title: authnd, an LDAP server for people who are somewhere else
item.description:
A site’s people are already in a database, a file or another directory. The things that want to authenticate them speak LDAP. authnd is the front: it binds and searches over go-authn/directory’s sources, so what a database holds can be read by anything that knows how to ask a directory. Pure Go, CGO_ENABLED=0, one binary. These pages describe v0.13.0, whose entries follow the standard schemas and pass the schema it serves at cn=Subschema, which a site extends with its own(SUPANN, eduPerson) and, withDIT content rules, name forms and structure rules,shapes, with go-authn/ldap v0.11.0 and go-authn/directory v0.15.0 under it; what is verified and what is not is on the status page.

Upgrading from v0.11.x

  • ⛔ Security: take v0.12.0, not v0.11.1. v0.11.1’s release binaries were built with Go 1.27.2, whose crypto/x509 does not distrust the compromised intermediate certificates GO-2026-6809 names, and authnd verifies certificates. v0.12.0 is built with Go 1.27.3, and its go directive is 1.27.3, so go install switches to the fixed toolchain by itself.
  • A configuration that does not use the new keys publishes what v0.11.1 published: a class is declared, never inferred, so without object_classes nothing changes.
  • New, all optional: schema_files and a schema block add a site’s definitions to the schema served, and object_classes andgroup_object_classes declare the auxiliary classes a source’s people and groups carry. A definition that redefines one already there is refused,even word for word, as slapd refuses it.
  • check and the startup log say which files and blocks were loaded, what each source declares, which classes were left off a person for lack of a MUST, and which groups two sources disagree about.

Run authnd check with the new binary before the restart, asinstall says.

Upgrading from v0.10.x

  • publish_nt_hash = true now needs a samba block,or authnd does not start.
  • A person without uidNumber, gidNumber and homeDirectory is no longer a posixAccount, and a group without a gidNumber no longer aposixGroup, so a consumer filtering on those classes sees fewer entries:see the entries.
  • A users "ldap" block reads more of the directory behind it by default:see people.

authnd check with the new binary says all three before the restart.

authnd --config /etc/authnd # serve
authnd check /etc/authnd # say what would be served, without listening

The smallest configuration 

listen = "127.0.0.1:3893" # the default
base_dn = "dc=example,dc=org" # required

reader "cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org" { password_file = "/etc/authnd/reader.pw" }

user "alice" { password_file = "/etc/authnd/passwords/alice.pw" }

group "staff" { members = ["alice"] }

People are published as uid=<name>,ou=people,<base_dn>, groups ascn=<name>,ou=groups,<base_dn>. What each entry is follows from what its source gave: a person is an account, or an inetOrgPerson when there is an sn, and a posixAccount only with uidNumber, gidNumber andhomeDirectory; every person is a uidObject. A group is a posixGroup (with memberUid) when it has a gidNumber, otherwise a groupOfNames (with member DNs), or an organizationalRole when it is also empty.sshPublicKey is added when the person has keys, and sambaNTPassword whenpublish_nt_hash says so and a SID can be given. Every entry passes the schema served atcn=Subschema before it is published: seethe entries and the schema. Up to v0.10.2 every person was a posixAccount and every group a posixGroup,whatever they had.

--config (-c) takes a file or a directory and may be repeated; a directory is every .hcl file in it, read in name order and merged into one configuration. A configuration with no base_dn, or with nobody in it, does not start.

Who may bind, and who may read

An LDAP server is asked to prove people, so its refusals are the design.These are answers from the v0.12.3 release binary to OpenLDAP’s own client:

$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin
dn:uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y wrong.pwin
ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49)
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -w ''
ldap_bind: Server is unwilling to perform (53)
additional info: an unauthenticated bind proves nothing, and this server does not accept one
$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -b dc=example,dc=org '(uid=alice)'
Insufficient access (50)
Additional information: only a reader may search
request answer why
empty name, empty password (RFC 4513 §5.1.1, anonymous) success it says “I am nobody”, which is true, and a client sends it before it has discovered anything
a name and an empty password (§5.1.2, unauthenticated) unwillingToPerform it names somebody and proves nothing; §5.1.2 asks for exactly this code. invalidCredentials would tell a person their password was wrong
a wrong password, or a name nobody here has invalidCredentials the two are not told apart
a search by anybody but a reader insufficientAccessRights binding proves who you are; reading everybody is a separate thing to be allowed
add, delete, modifyDN unwillingToPerform no handler is wired for them; the one write is a person’s own password

A reader is a service account with a bind DN and password orpassword_file; a reader with neither is refused at startup (a reader that proves nothing is anonymous search with extra steps). Without any reader,nothing may search, and check says so.

The root DSE is answered to an anonymous client, as discovery needs:

$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -s base -b '' '+' '*'
dn:
objectClass: top
objectClass: OpenLDAProotDSE
supportedLDAPVersion: 3
namingContexts: dc=example,dc=org
supportedExtension: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.3
supportedExtension: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.1
supportedControl: 1.2.840.113556.1.4.319
supportedControl: 1.3.6.1.1.13.1
supportedControl: 1.3.6.1.1.13.2
supportedFeatures: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.1
supportedFeatures: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.3
subschemaSubentry: cn=Subschema
vendorName: go-authn/authnd
vendorVersion: v0.13.0

1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.1 is the RFC 3062 password modify operation.subschemaSubentry names the schema,which is answered to an anonymous client as well.supportedSASLMechanisms: OAUTHBEARER appears only with anoidc block.

Where to go next

Installing it the release binary, the authnd account, the systemd unit, upgrades
Where the people come from user and group blocks, a SQL database, another LDAP directory
The entries and the schema what each person and group is published as, cn=Subschema, attributes, what is dropped or withheld
Site schemas schema_files, the schema block and object_classes: SUPANN, eduPerson or a site’s own attributes; DIT content rules, name forms and DIT structure rules
check read the configuration back before restarting
TLS ldaps:// or StartTLS, and publish_nt_hash
Changing a password ldappasswd, ldapmodify, and why the old password is always asked for
A Kerberos realm the keytab, and who can be issued a ticket
A second factor a one-time code on the end of the password
A token at the bind OIDC over SASL OAUTHBEARER
Running it signals, restarts, what it logs, how to tell it is up

About the transcripts

Every command shown on these pages was run again on 2026-10-26 with the release binaries, not retyped: authnd v0.12.3 (authnd-darwin-arm64, checked by relverify against SHA256SUMS and its attestation; go version -m: go1.27.3, mod github.com/go-authn/authnd v0.12.3, vcs.modified=false), authn-bridge v0.23.4, authn-revokd v0.6.6, sshcert-authorize v0.1.9 and ldapschema v0.10.1. What the commands printed is what stands here. Two transcripts are exceptions, and each says so where it stands: the oidctool client of the token page, a test client written for these pages and part of no release, whose transcripts and the server lines beside them were printed by the v0.10.0 release binary; and RENATER’s expired metadata on the federation page, a file that is no longer published. All of them were asked by the OpenLDAP and Heimdal clients that ship with macOS, on 127.0.0.1 on unprivileged ports, in a scratch directory. That is why the configurations behind them name files by relative paths such as etc/authnd/passwords/alice.pw, and why the password files have names like alice.pwin. The /etc/authnd paths in the examples are what an installed server uses. The transcripts that print the version of authnd were run again with v0.13.0 (authnd-darwin-arm64, checked by relverify against SHA256SUMS and its attestation; go version -m: go1.27.3, mod github.com/go-authn/authnd v0.13.0): the root DSE here and on the operations page, and authnd --version. The schema of the entries page was printed by v0.12.4 (mod github.com/go-authn/authnd v0.12.4, vcs.modified=false); v0.13.0 prints no value of dITContentRules, nameForms or dITStructureRules for a schema without rules, which was checked. The rules section of the site schemas page says what it was run with.

item.title: Where the people come from
item.description:
A user block is the whole directory for a small site, or the service accounts a big one keeps out of its database. A site whose people are already in a database or in LDAP should not copy them into a second place that goes stale, so a users block reads them where they are. The users block is go-authn/directory’s hcldir, the same onego-fileshare reads: one directory is described the same way to both.

Written in the configuration 

user "alice" { password_file = "/etc/authnd/passwords/alice.pw" }

user "carol" {
 nt_hash = "…" # MD4(UTF16LE(password)), 32 hex
 authorized_keys = ["ssh-ed25519 AAAA… carol@laptop"] # published as sshPublicKey
}

group "staff" { members = ["alice", "carol"] }
field what it is
password the password, inline
password_file the same, read from a file (surrounding white space removed)
nt_hash MD4(UTF16LE(password)), 32 hex characters — for a site that holds that and not the password
totp_secret a base32 one-time-code secret, at least 128 bits; see a second factor
authorized_keys authorized_keys lines, published as sshPublicKey
authorized_keys_file the same, from a file
attributes from v0.11.0, what describes the person and proves nothing — sn, uidNumber, gidNumber, homeDirectory, mail… — as a map of strings or lists of strings; a group block takes it too. They decide what the entry is published as: see the entries
object_classes from v0.12.0, the auxiliary classes this person (or, in a group block, this group) is published with, such as ["siteMember"]: declared, never inferred, and defined in a site schema

Refused at startup, naming the person:

  • password and password_file together — say which one;
  • password and nt_hash together — the hash is derived from the password,so two of them can disagree;
  • authorized_keys and authorized_keys_file together;
  • an nt_hash that is not 32 hex characters, an authorized_keys line that does not parse, a totp_secret under 128 bits;
  • the same user or group twice, and a group with no members.

A group member that no source knows is refused too, which is what catches a typo before it silently grants nothing:

$ authnd check cases/typo.hcl
authnd: group "staff" has "alise" in it, who is not in the configuration file

An nt_hash alone cannot bind

A person written with only nt_hash is published, can be handed to an SMB server through sambaNTPassword, and cannot bind to authnd itself: an LDAP simple bind sends the password, and an NT hash is not a way to check one here. bob below has only an NT hash, and the hash is that of the password sent:

$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=bob,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y bob.pwin
ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49)

check says so, after the tables:

bob and eli cannot bind with a password: their sources hold only what an SMB server needs (an NT hash), which a bind cannot be checked against

Why it is refused, by design. An NT hash is MD4(UTF16LE(password)),unsalted and fast (MS-NLMP §3.3.1, NTOWFv1). Accepting it to check LDAP binds would widen what a leaked hash opens, from SMB to every application that binds through authnd. Kerberos refuses these people for a related reason: the NT hash is the RC4-HMAC key (RFC 4757 §2), and the realm issues AES only. This is a deliberate decision, not a missing feature, and there is no option to change it.

What to do instead. When migrating from a directory that holds only NT hashes (Samba, an exported AD), give each person a real password or a password check in their source: a password reset, or a users "ldap" source whose upstream directory checks the password itself. Do not keep the NT hash as the only credential.

In a SQL database 

users "sql" {
 driver = "postgres" # or mysql (mariadb), or sqlite
 dsn_file = "/etc/authnd/pg.dsn" # required: a DSN may hold a password
 users = "select login, secret, nt_hash from staff" # required
 groups = "select team, member from team_members" # optional
}

The queries are yours, because a site’s people are already in that site’s shape. The users query’s columns are read by position: a name,then any of a password, an NT hash, SSH keys (one per line) and a one-time-code secret, in that order — up to five columns. A NULL is a credential that person does not have. A password column is compared as it is stored: authnd has no setting for a hashed column. The groups query returns a group name and a member, one row per membership.

Two more queries, optional, read attributes by column alias rather than by position: users_attributes (a name, then one column per attribute) andgroups_attributes (a group, then the same). An unquoted alias is lower-cased by PostgreSQL. See the entries.

The classes of what a users block gives are declared beside its queries(from v0.12.0, the same two keys in a users "ldap" block):

users "sql" {
 # ...
 object_classes = ["supannPerson", "eduPerson"] # every person this block gives
 group_object_classes = ["supannGroupe"] # every group
}

Each must be an AUXILIARY class that the schema served defines (the standard schema, or schema_files and a schema block),and not one authnd derives itself. A person missing a MUST of a declared class is published without it, and check says so.

driver accepts postgres (or postgresql, pgx), mysql (or mariadb)and sqlite (or sqlite3). The database is reached at startup, before anything listens, so one that is not answering stops the server where somebody is watching:

$ authnd check cases/nodb
authnd: users "sql": the postgres database is not answering: failed to connect to `user=authnd database=authnd`:
127.0.0.1:1 (127.0.0.1): dial error: dial tcp 127.0.0.1:1: connect: connection refused
127.0.0.1:1 (127.0.0.1): dial error: dial tcp 127.0.0.1:1: connect: connection refused

PostgreSQL on the same machine through its socket and peer authentication needs no password in the DSN: host=/run/postgresql dbname=authnd user=authnd.SQLite in the state directory: file:/var/lib/authnd/people.db.

A key that belongs to the other kind of block is refused rather than ignored:

$ authnd check cases/sqlwrongkey.hcl
authnd: users "sql" has base_dn in it, which belongs to an ldap block

In another LDAP directory 

users "ldap" {
 url = "ldaps://ldap.example.org"
 base_dn = "ou=people,dc=example,dc=org"
 bind_dn = "cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org"
 bind_password_file = "/etc/authnd/upstream.pw"
}

url and base_dn are required. Where the people and groups are, and which attributes name them:

key default
user_filter (|(objectClass=posixAccount)(objectClass=account)(objectClass=uidObject))
user_attribute uid
group_base_dn base_dn
group_filter (|(objectClass=posixGroup)(objectClass=groupOfNames))
group_attribute cn
group_member_attribute none: memberUid (names) and member (DNs); set, it is the one attribute read
totp_attribute none: there is no standard attribute, and a guess would read nothing while looking like it had looked
attributes, group_attributes none: the attributes to copy from each person’s entry and each group’s, such as ["mail", "uidNumber", "homeDirectory"] and ["gidNumber"] (the entries)
object_classes, group_object_classes none: from v0.12.0, the auxiliary classes every person and every group read from this directory is published with (site schemas); the classes the upstream entries carry are never copied
start_tls false

A member DN counts only when it is the DN of an entry the people search returned: a DN outside them, or naming nobody, maps to nobody, and the name is never read out of the DN. sambaNTPassword and sshPublicKey are read under those names.

From v0.11.0 the defaults read more of an institution’s directory

The block is go-authn/directory’s, and directory v0.14.0, which authnd v0.11.0 embeds, widened its defaults: up to v0.10.2, user_filter was(objectClass=posixAccount), group_filter (objectClass=posixGroup) andgroup_member_attribute memberUid. A directory holding account oruidObject entries that are not posixAccounts — service accounts, hosts named by uid, people imported from elsewhere — now gives them to authnd, and each can be checked by a bind; its groupOfNames groups become groups here.To keep exactly the old set, write the old values:

users "ldap" {
 # ...
 user_filter = "(objectClass=posixAccount)"
 group_filter = "(objectClass=posixGroup)"
 group_member_attribute = "memberUid"
}

Two things are refused before anything is opened:

$ authnd check cases/ldap-clear.hcl
authnd: users "ldap" would send every password to "ldap.example.org" in the clear: use ldaps://, or start_tls = true (RFC 4513 §5.1.3)
$ authnd check cases/ldap-cred.hcl
authnd: users "ldap" has credentials in its url, and a url is printed: use bind_dn with bind_password_file

ldap:// to a loopback address and ldapi:// are accepted: nobody is on the way.

A directory behind this one checks passwords by binding to it; it does not hand them over. Here one authnd fronts another, under a different base;the one behind is the check example, served on 3893:

listen = "127.0.0.1:3894"
base_dn = "dc=example,dc=net"

users "ldap" {
 url = "ldap://127.0.0.1:3893"
 base_dn = "ou=people,dc=example,dc=org"
 group_base_dn = "ou=groups,dc=example,dc=org"
 bind_dn = "cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org"
 bind_password_file = "etc/authnd/reader.pw"
}

user "svc-backup" { password_file = "etc/authnd/svc-backup.pw" }
$ authnd check front2
ldap://127.0.0.1:3894, base dc=example,dc=net
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH
alice ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 a password check account, uidObject uid
bob ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 a password check account, uidObject uid
dora ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 a password check account, uidObject uid
eli ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 a password check account, uidObject uid
svc-backup the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid
GROUP MEMBERS PUBLISHED AS
engineers dora and eli groupOfNames
staff alice, bob and dora groupOfNames
alice has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
bob has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
dora has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
eli has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
svc-backup has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
group engineers has no gidNumber: not a posixGroup, published as a groupOfNames (member DNs, no memberUid)
group staff has no gidNumber: not a posixGroup, published as a groupOfNames (member DNs, no memberUid)
a bind carries a password
no reader is declared: nothing may search, and binds are not affected
sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it)
this configuration can be served

Every person the directory behind publishes is an account and every group a groupOfNames, since none has POSIX attributes: the defaults read them,and the groups’ member DNs map to the people imported. With the defaults up to v0.10.2, (objectClass=posixAccount) would have matched none of them.

A password check is enough for a bind, and is never enough for aKerberos ticket or for SMB.

Order, and the one exception

Sources are asked in the order they are written, and the first one that knows a name owns it. The user blocks always come first, so a service account written down locally is not overridden by somebody with the same name in the database. Group membership is the union of every source: a group that a group block and a database’s groups query both name has the members of both.

Two names that differ only by case are refused

A uid is compared ignoring case (RFC 4519 §2.39), and so is every DN, soDora in the file and dora in a database are one name to LDAP and two people to anything that compares bytes — a password change by one would land on the other. Such a configuration does not start:

$ authnd check cases/case.hcl
authnd: "Dora" (from the configuration file) and "dora" (from a sqlite database) differ only by case, and an LDAP name does not tell them apart: a uid is compared ignoring case. Rename one of them

Read once

Every source is read once, at startup. A person added to the database, or a membership changed in the directory behind this one, is served after a restart, not before. That includes a password column in a database: it is read with the rest of the row. A directory behind this one is different only in that a bind is checked by binding to it, so a password changed there is the one that works. The other exception is a password a person changes through authnd itself, which is applied at once.There is no reload; see running it.

item.title: The entries authnd publishes, and the schema it serves
item.description:
Every entry authnd publishes passes the schema it serves. From v0.11.0 each person and group is a standard-schema entry, built from what its source gave, and checked with go-authn/ldap’s schema.Validate against the schema a client can read at cn=Subschema before it is ever returned by a search. A client that reads the schema and believes it — an LDAP browser, a synchronisation tool, a directory replicating this one — is shown what it was told. Up to v0.10.2 every person was top, person, posixAccount with none of the attributes those classes require, and sambaNTPassword sat on an entry with no class that allows it.

A consumer filtering on posixAccount or posixGroup sees fewer entries

A person without uidNumber, gidNumber and homeDirectory is no longer aposixAccount, and a group without a gidNumber is no longer aposixGroup. A program that searches (objectClass=posixAccount) or(objectClass=posixGroup) no longer finds them. That includes go-authn/directory’s ldapdir up to v0.13.0, and so go-fileshare until it requires directory v0.14.0, whose defaults also read account, uidObject and groupOfNames (directory).Give people and groups those attributes, or point the consumer at(objectClass=uidObject), which every person carries.

The shapes

Every superclass is listed, as RFC 4512 §3.3 asks.

a person with… objectClass cn
no sn top, account (RFC 4524 §3.1) only when another class allows it
sn top, person, organizationalPerson, inetOrgPerson (RFC 4519, RFC 2798) yes
… and uidNumber, gidNumber, homeDirectory, all three + posixAccount (RFC 2307) yes
… and SSH keys + ldapPublicKey (openssh-lpk), with sshPublicKey
… and a published NT hash with a sambaSID + sambaSamAccount (Samba), with sambaSID and sambaNTPassword: see the samba block allowed
… always + uidObject (RFC 4519 §3.14), so (objectClass=uidObject) finds everybody
a group with… objectClass members
a gidNumber top, posixGroup (RFC 2307) memberUid, names
no gidNumber, somebody in it top, groupOfNames (RFC 4519 §3.5) member, the DNs this server publishes
no gidNumber, nobody in it top, organizationalRole (RFC 4519 §3.10) none
a gidNumber, nobody in it top, posixGroup none: an attribute has at least one value

uid is the person’s name, and so is cn wherever a class allows it. Anaccount alone does not allow cn (its MAY is description, seeAlso,l, o, ou and host), so a person without sn and without the POSIX trio carries uid and no cn.

Why these choices, from authnd’s own reasons:

  • posixGroup follows RFC 2307, not draft-howard-rfc2307bis-02. The draft makes posixGroup AUXILIARY and expired unpublished; an AUXILIARYposixGroup would need a structural class beside it, groupOfNames, whosemember an empty group cannot give.
  • organizationalRole for an empty group without a gidNumber. groupOfNames and groupOfUniqueNames both require a member, and the ways of inventing one are false: member: "" names the root DSE, and the group’s own DN makes it a member of itself. organizationalRole is the one standard structural class whose only MUST is cn, and it takesdescription, ou and seeAlso as groupOfNames does.
  • Auxiliary classes without DIT content rules. RFC 4512 §2.4.3 forbids auxiliary classes on an entry whose structural class has no DIT content rule. Every directory server in use allows them, and so does Validate (ValidateOptions{StrictAuxiliary: true} is the strict reading, and authnd does not set it). A class whose structural class has a content rule is held to it from v0.13.0: see the rules.

Adding attributes

What a source says about somebody that proves nothing — a uidNumber, a home directory, a mail address — is an attribute, published as given.They are go-authn/directory’s attributes,from v0.13.0, and they are kept apart from credentials: a name that holds a secret, or one the server derives itself, is refused before anything is read.

In a user or group block 

user "dora" {
 password_file = "/etc/authnd/passwords/dora.pw"
 authorized_keys = ["ssh-ed25519 AAAA… dora@laptop"]
 attributes = {
 sn = "Explorer" # inetOrgPerson
 uidNumber = "1000" # the three: posixAccount
 gidNumber = "1000"
 homeDirectory = "/home/dora"
 mail = ["dora@example.org", "d.explorer@example.org"]
 }
}

group "engineers" {
 members = ["dora", "eli"]
 attributes = { gidNumber = "2000" } # a posixGroup; without it, a groupOfNames
}

A value is a string or a list of strings; null leaves the attribute out.A number is refused, because an LDAP value is a string and authnd does not choose how a number is spelled:

$ authnd check cases/number.hcl
authnd: user "alice": attributes: uidNumber is the number 1000: write it as a string, "1000" -- an LDAP value is a string, and this does not choose how a number is spelled
$ authnd check cases/secret.hcl
authnd: user "alice": attributes: directory: not an attribute this package carries: "userPassword" holds a secret, and attributes are published: a credential has its own option or none

Refused the same way, whatever their case: any name holding a secret(userPassword, sambaNTPassword, unicodePwd, krbPrincipalKey and the rest of go-authn/directory’s list, or any name containing password,passwd, pwd, secret, credential, hash or privatekey);sshPublicKey, which has authorized_keys; uid, cn and objectClass,which the server derives; member, memberUid and the other membership attributes, which members answers; the operational attributes a server maintains; and a name in numeric form (2.5.4.35 is userPassword).

In a SQL database

Two optional queries of a users "sql" block read attributes by column alias. The first column is the person’s or the group’s name; every other column is an attribute named by its alias:

users "sql" {
 driver = "sqlite"
 dsn_file = "/etc/authnd/people.dsn"
 users = "select login, secret, null, ssh_keys from staff"
 groups = "select team, member from teams"
 users_attributes = "select login, sn, uid as uidNumber, gid as gidNumber, home as homeDirectory, mail from person_attrs"
 groups_attributes = "select team, gid as gidNumber, description from team_attrs"
}
  • The positional users and groups queries are unchanged, and a sixth positional column is still refused: attributes come by name, in their own query.
  • A column whose alias is not an attribute description (an unaliased expression such as count(*)), or names a credential, is refused with its column number before a row is read.
  • NULL and '' are absent. A name may come back on several rows, and the values of all of them are kept, so a join to a table of addresses gives a person several.
  • A group named only in groups_attributes exists, with nobody in it:that is how a person’s own primary group is written.

The case of an alias is the database’s

PostgreSQL folds an unquoted alias to lower case: as uidNumber comes back as uidnumber. Attribute names are case-insensitive, so it is the same attribute and the entry is the same entry to every LDAP client, but the spelling authnd prints is the database’s. Quote the alias where the spelling matters: gid as "gidNumber". SQLite keeps an alias as written.

From another LDAP directory

A users "ldap" block copies the attributes it is told to, from each person’s entry and each group’s: attributes = ["mail", "uidNumber", "homeDirectory"] and group_attributes = ["gidNumber"]. Seepeople.

A configuration, and what it publishes

The SQL block above, with a reader, over a SQLite database of five people and four groups, as the v0.11.0 release binary checks it:

listen = "127.0.0.1:3893"
base_dn = "dc=example,dc=org"

reader "cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org" { password_file = "etc/authnd/reader.pw" }

users "sql" {
 driver = "sqlite"
 dsn_file = "etc/authnd/people.dsn"
 users = "select login, secret, null, ssh_keys from staff"
 groups = "select team, member from teams"
 users_attributes = "select login, sn, uid as uidNumber, gid as gidNumber, home as homeDirectory, mail from person_attrs"
 groups_attributes = "select team, gid as gidNumber, description from team_attrs"
}
$ authnd check etc/authnd
ldap://127.0.0.1:3893, base dc=example,dc=org
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH

Which class finds whom:

$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b dc=example,dc=org '(objectClass=uidObject)' 1.1

What is dropped, and what is withheld

given the entry why
uidNumber, gidNumber, no homeDirectory, no sn account, uidObject, without the two no class of the entry allows it; posixAccount would
mail, no sn account, uidObject, without it no class of the entry allows it; inetOrgPerson would
a type the schema does not define the rest the schema served here does not define it
mail on a group without a gidNumber groupOfNames, without it

a gidNumber that is not an integer withheld: not of its syntax

Only what a source gave is dropped, and which attribute is not allowed is Validate’s answer, not a second reading of the schema. The entry is validated again after dropping. An entry that still fails is withheld:it is absent from every search, the startup log names it, and check lists it with every problem Validate found. An attribute authnd derives itself(uid, cn, objectClass, sshPublicKey, sambaSID, sambaNTPassword)that the schema refused would be a defect in authnd, and withholds the entry rather than publish it without.

alice’s gidNumber is a word here:

listen = "127.0.0.1:3893"

$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b dc=example,dc=org '(uid=alice)'

What is withheld is the entry a search returns, not the identity.

The schema it serves

The root DSE names it (subschemaSubentry: cn=Subschema, onthe root DSE),and a base search of cn=Subschema returns it (RFC 4512 §4.2): the standard definitions go-authn/ldap embeds — RFC 4512, 4517, 4519, 4523,4524, 2798, 2307, 3672 and 3045, and openssh-lpk — plus Samba’ssambaSamAccount, sambaSID and sambaNTPassword when there is asamba block. The definitions are published only when asked for by name or with +. Trimmed where marked:

$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -o ldif-wrap=no -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -s base -b cn=Subschema '+' '*'

objectClass: subentry
objectClass: subschema
cn: Subschema

ldapSyntaxes: ( 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.3 DESC 'Attribute Type Description' )
[...]

[...]

[...]

[...]

[...]

[...]

The whole entry was 327 lines: 49 syntaxes, 40 matching rules, 36 matching rule uses, 143 attribute types and 52 object classes. Unlike a search under the base, the subschema entry, like the root DSE, is answered to an anonymous client: the same query without -D and -y returned it.

Filters use the schema’s matching rules, so (uidNumber>=1000) compares integers. uidNumber and gidNumber have ORDERING integerOrderingMatch, which RFC 2307 does not give them; slapd and draft-howard-rfc2307bis-02 do, and so does go-authn/ldap(its one departure).As strings, 1000 sorts before 999:

$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b dc=example,dc=org '(uidNumber>=1000)' uidNumber

uidNumber: 1000
dn: uid=eli,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
uidNumber: 1001

hal is not there: hal’s uidNumber was dropped. A range on an attribute with no ORDERING rule, such as uid, is Undefined and matches nothing.

item.title: Site schemas, and the classes a source declares
item.description:
A SUPANN or eduPerson attribute is dropped unless a class of its entry allows it. authnd publishes only what the schema it serves permits (seethe entries),and the standard schema knows nothing of supannEtablissement oreduPersonAffiliation. From v0.12.0 a site says three things, in this order:

  1. which definitions to add: schema_files, the files its slapd already loads, and a schema { } block for what is only local;
  2. which auxiliary classes its people and groups carry: object_classes;
  3. nothing else. A class is declared, never inferred: an attribute appearing in a database does not change what an entry is published as.

The example on this page is an example

example.schema below was written for this page. Its OIDs are under1.3.6.1.4.1.99999, an arc nobody is assigned: use your own, and never copy these. For SUPANN, see the end of the page.

An example: a schema, a database, a configuration

A schema in OpenLDAP’s .schema form: one class a source can declare(exampleStaff, AUXILIARY, with a MUST), and one it cannot(exampleUnit, STRUCTURAL).

objectidentifier exampleRoot 1.3.6.1.4.1.99999
objectidentifier exampleAttr exampleRoot:1
objectidentifier exampleClass exampleRoot:2
attributetype ( exampleAttr:1 NAME 'exampleBadge'
DESC 'the number on a badge'
EQUALITY caseIgnoreMatch
SYNTAX 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.15
SINGLE-VALUE )
attributetype ( exampleAttr:2 NAME 'exampleEmployeeId'
DESC 'a staff number'
EQUALITY caseExactMatch
SYNTAX 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.15
SINGLE-VALUE )
# AUXILIARY: it can be declared. exampleStaff has a MUST.
objectclass ( exampleClass:1 NAME 'exampleStaff' SUP top AUXILIARY
DESC 'somebody employed: has a staff number'
MUST exampleEmployeeId
MAY exampleBadge )
# STRUCTURAL: it cannot be declared (an entry has one structural chain).
objectclass ( exampleClass:2 NAME 'exampleUnit' SUP top STRUCTURAL
MUST cn )

A SQLite database of three people, with sn, a badge and a staff number(sqlite3 var/people.db < people.sql):

create table staff (login text primary key, secret text);
create table person_attrs (login text primary key, sn text, badge text, empid text, locker text);
insert into staff values ('ann', 'ann-password'), ('ben', 'ben-password'), ('cat', 'cat-password');
insert into person_attrs values ('ann', 'Archer', 'B-0001', 'E-1001', 'L-12'), ('ben', 'Brook', 'B-0002', null, null), ('cat', 'Cole', null, 'E-1003', null);

And the configuration:

listen = "127.0.0.1:3893"
base_dn = "dc=example,dc=org"

reader "cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org" { password_file = "etc/authnd/reader.pw" }

# Files first, then the blocks: a definition may use anything before it.
schema_files = ["etc/authnd/example.schema"]

schema {
 attribute_type "exampleLocker" {
 oid = "1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.1.3"
 syntax = "1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.15"
 }
 object_class "exampleLockerHolder" {
 oid = "1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.2.3"
 kind = "auxiliary"
 may = ["exampleLocker"]
 }
}

users "sql" {
 driver = "sqlite"
 dsn_file = "etc/authnd/people.dsn"
 users = "select login, secret from staff"
 users_attributes = "select login, sn, badge as exampleBadge, empid as exampleEmployeeId, locker as exampleLocker from person_attrs"
 object_classes = ["exampleStaff", "exampleLockerHolder"] # declared, never inferred
}

Without the object_classes line, check says what the standard schema alone does with the same people: the attributes are dropped, and each line names the class that would have kept it.

$ authnd check cases/nodecl.hcl
ldap://127.0.0.1:3893, base dc=example,dc=org
schema: etc/authnd/example.schema adds 3 object identifier macros, 2 attribute types and 2 object classes
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH
ann a sqlite database a password person, organizationalPerson, inetOrgPerson, uidObject uid, cn and sn
ben a sqlite database a password person, organizationalPerson, inetOrgPerson, uidObject uid, cn and sn
cat a sqlite database a password person, organizationalPerson, inetOrgPerson, uidObject uid, cn and sn
ann has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as person, organizationalPerson, inetOrgPerson, uidObject
ann is published without exampleBadge: no class of the entry allows it; exampleStaff would
ann is published without exampleEmployeeId: no class of the entry allows it; exampleStaff would
ben has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as person, organizationalPerson, inetOrgPerson, uidObject
ben is published without exampleBadge: no class of the entry allows it; exampleStaff would
cat has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as person, organizationalPerson, inetOrgPerson, uidObject
cat is published without exampleEmployeeId: no class of the entry allows it; exampleStaff would
a bind carries a password
cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org may search; every other bound client may not
sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it)
this configuration can be served

schema_files

schema_files is a list of OpenLDAP .schema files or cn=config LDIF files.They are loaded as published, in order, on top of the standard schema (and Samba’s three definitions, with the samba block), by go-authn/ldap’s slapd-compatible readers:any order of terms, slapd and RFC 2849 continuations, base64, {N} length prefixes, and objectidentifier macros, which one file may define and the next use, as across slapd’s include. Nothing is converted beforehand, so the file a site’s slapd loads is the file authnd loads. The definitions are served atcn=Subschema.

  • A relative path is relative to the working directory, as every other path in the configuration is. Use absolute paths in a service: the working directory of a systemd unit is /.

  • Each file must be a regular file of at most 4 MiB, and is read once, at startup.

  • The files decide what every entry may hold. They are not secrets, but keep them with the rest of the configuration: root:authnd, mode 0640, in a directory only root writes (install).

  • A file that does not build refuses startup, and check, with the file, the line and the column where the definition starts, and the kind of refusal at the end of the message: an unknown superclass, attribute, matching rule or syntax (unknown reference), a structural class derived from an auxiliary one (kind violation), an OID or a name defined twice (duplicate OID,duplicate name). Since v0.12.1 the place and the kind come from go-authn/ldap’s typed*schema.BuildError, not from reading its message. A definition read from a file starts at column 1,also when its text is folded over several lines. A duplicate says where its first definition is, and a redefinition says which standard file, or which line of an earlier file, holds the original. Two examples:

    cases/unknown.schema has a MAY that is defined nowhere:

    # exampleB has a MAY that is defined nowhere.
objectclass ( 1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.2.9 NAME 'exampleB' SUP top AUXILIARY
MAY noSuchAttribute )
    $ authnd check cases/unknown.hcl
authnd: schema_files: cases/unknown.schema:2:1: the object class exampleB has MAY noSuchAttribute, which is not a defined attribute type (unknown reference)

    cases/twice.schema gives one OID to two attribute types:

    attributetype ( 1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.1.9 NAME 'exampleA'
SYNTAX 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.15 )
attributetype ( 1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.1.9 NAME 'exampleB'
SYNTAX 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.15 )
    $ authnd check cases/twice.hcl
authnd: schema_files: cases/twice.schema:4:1: the attribute type 1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.1.9 is defined twice (first defined at cases/twice.schema:1:1) (duplicate OID)

A redefinition is refused, even an identical one

A file may not define what is already there: the standard schema’s definitions, Samba’s, or an earlier file’s. It is refused even word for word, which is slapd’s own rule: a schema file’s definitions go throughparse_at and parse_oc, and slapd answers an OID or a name already indexed with Duplicate attributeType (same OID and names) or Inconsistent duplicate attributeType (servers/slapd/at.c, oc.c). Only slapd’s own hard-coded schema is allowed the first. A file slapd refuses is a file authnd refuses.

The other reading would have to pick a winner, and that is a silent change to what every client is told a standard attribute is; refusing names the line instead. The refusal says whether the text was the same. A file that redefines cn (2.5.4.3) with a definition of its own:

$ authnd check cases/dup.hcl
authnd: schema_files: cases/cn-copy.schema:1:1: the attribute type cn (2.5.4.3) is already defined by the standard schema (rfc4519.schema:42:1), and this is a different definition: a schema file adds definitions and never replaces one -- slapd refuses this too ("Duplicate attributeType", servers/slapd/at.c and oc.c). Remove it from this file

The schema { } block

For definitions that are only local, a schema block holds them in HCL2, in hclschema’s shape:attribute_type, object_class, object_identifier, matching_rule andldap_syntax. It is read after the files, so it may use their definitions, and there may be several.

Values must be literals: no variables, no functions, no ${...} or%{...}. The block is decoded by the same decoder that reads an .hcl schema file, with the same bounds, and every error names the configuration’s own line and column. A block that is not in HCL’s native syntax is refused.

object_classes

A definition in the schema allows an attribute; it does not put the class on anybody. A source declares the auxiliary classes its people and groups are published with:

where key what it declares
users block, any kind object_classes the classes of every person the block gives
users block, any kind group_object_classes the classes of every group
user block object_classes the classes of that person
group block object_classes the classes of that group 
users "sql" {
 # ...
 object_classes = ["supannPerson", "eduPerson"]
 group_object_classes = ["supannGroupe"]
}

user "alice" { object_classes = ["siteMember"] }
group "staff" { object_classes = ["supannGroupe"] }

These keys are go-authn/directory’s, from v0.15.0(library). Names are compared ignoring case, and kept once, in the order written.

What authnd does with a declared class:

  • It is published with its superclasses, after the classes authnd derives(RFC 4512 §3.3: all the superclasses of the named classes are implicitly added). The attributes the class allows are kept instead of dropped.
  • It is never inferred. A person whose source declares nothing keeps losing the attributes no class of theirs allows, whatever the database holds.
  • A person missing a MUST of a declared class is published without that class. Its attributes are dropped like any attribute no class allows, and both are reported. That is the rule authnd follows everywhere: the person stays published, the problem is said, nothing is changed silently.Withholding the person would take them out of every search for one missing attribute; publishing the class without its MUST would serve an entry that fails the schema served.
  • Two sources may declare different classes for one group. The first source that declares classes for a group decides, whole, and a later list is ignored: neither merged nor an error. check says so.

Here ann has everything, cat has no locker (a MAY), and ben has noexampleEmployeeId, a MUST of exampleStaff:

$ authnd check etc/authnd
ldap://127.0.0.1:3893, base dc=example,dc=org
schema: etc/authnd/example.schema adds 3 object identifier macros, 2 attribute types and 2 object classes
schema: the schema block at etc/authnd/authnd.hcl:9:1 adds 1 attribute type and 1 object class: exampleLocker and exampleLockerHolder
etc/authnd/authnd.hcl:26:22: users "sql" declares exampleStaff and exampleLockerHolder for its people
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH

$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -o ldif-wrap=no -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y etc/authnd/reader.pw -b ou=people,dc=example,dc=org '(uid=*)'
